header.competitor: Unnamed competitor (never named in the interview)
header.incumbent: Unnamed payments provider whose support was a ticket form
header.tag_why: The decider rejected our tiered support as "a queue with a faster timer". The competitor put a named solutions engineer and account lead in the room, and Ben says they promised on-call coverage for every major on-sale.

messaging_changes.current_line: Support plans with tiered response times, up to 24/7 coverage.
messaging_changes.change: For the operations owner (e.g. COO) in ticketing and peak-event deals: "A name, not a queue." Lead with the named people on the account, such as [solutions engineer] and [account lead], and the escalation path we commit to for the customer's major events. Do not open with tiers or response times; mention them only if asked.
messaging_changes.why: When Halima asked "who's my person," the rep walked her through the support plans and she dismissed them as "a queue with a faster timer," so M5's tiered-response framing answered a who question with a how-fast answer.

messaging_changes.change: Add a written on-sale morning plan as a proof asset for peak-event buyers, built with the solutions engineer before the decider meeting. It should cover who's watching, who you call, and what we do at minute one, minute four and minute ten of a payment failure.
messaging_changes.why: The decider wanted to see on paper "what we do on an on-sale morning" down to "what happens at minute four," the moment her own payments failed, and the rep says we don't have that as a thing.

messaging_changes.current_line: Financial infrastructure to grow globally, in every currency.
messaging_changes.change: For ticketing and peak-event deals, open with the outage moment rather than global growth: "I don't buy uptime, I buy what happens when it's down." Then state what we do in the first minutes of a failure on on-sale morning. Keep M2 for the technical evaluator.
messaging_changes.why: The trigger was a public on-sale failure with no human reply until it was over, and the decider explicitly said she buys what happens when it's down; the technical story got only a "good" from her.

messaging_changes.current_line: Trusted by leading businesses; see our customer stories.
messaging_changes.change: For peak-event operations buyers, swap logo stories for a reference customer who will speak directly to how we responded during an incident, including who picked up and what happened next.
messaging_changes.why: The rep said "I had logos. I didn't have a person," and the buyer wanted a name, so brand proof did not answer her question. Whether she explicitly asked for a reference is still unconfirmed.

trigger.insight: Payments had failed during on-sales before, and nobody switched. The trigger was a failure the CEO saw in public, made worse because no human answered until the on-sale was over. From the first day this was a buy about the response during an outage, not about the platform. The person who set the mandate was the COO, not the CTO.
trigger.messaging: Open ticketing and peak-event deals with what happens in the first minutes of a failure on on-sale morning, not with M1's global-growth line.

decider.insight: The rep knows the decider only through the champion, and the champion openly lost the argument inside his own company. Our story was built for the CTO, while the COO who owned the mandate from the trigger onward was buying something else. It is unclear which meeting she decided in, or what was said in it.
decider.messaging: In peak-event deals, write a separate operations-owner narrative for the COO about on-sale risk and accountability, alongside the CTO's technical narrative.

competitor.insight: The competitor won by putting real people in the room, not by showing features. Ben reports the on-call promise, so it is the customer's account, not a verified capability. The rep's theory that they over-promised is unverified, and he admits it. It also misses the point: Halima bought a name she could hold to account, and we never offered a counter-commitment she could test. The competitor's name and whether Halima attended that meeting were never established.
competitor.messaging: Stop competing on response-time tiers. Name the people on the account and state exactly what coverage we commit to for the customer's major events.

gaps.insight: These were proof gaps, not product gaps. There was no written event-day runbook and no ticketing reference who could say who picked up. The rep says the first could have been assembled with our solutions engineer. Her phrase minute four points straight back at the trigger failure, so she was asking us to replay her worst day with us in it. M8's logos-and-stories approach fails here because she wanted a person, not a brand.
gaps.messaging: Build a standard on-sale or peak-event plan (who watches, who to call, what we do in minute one through minute ten), and add reference customers who will speak to an incident response, not just logo stories.

language.insight: Their vocabulary is people and moments: who, a name, someone who picks up, on-sale morning. Ours is categories and metrics: support plans, tiers, uptime. Her line about not buying uptime rejects the reliability claim behind our technical story, and the support category name itself was ours, never hers.
language.messaging: Use their words in peak-event messaging: lead with a name, not a queue, and with what happens when it's down, and drop support-plan tier language from the opening.

gaps.follow_up: Ask Jordan whether Halima or Ben requested a reference customer, and in what words.

close.rep_takeaway: Your technical win was real, but it was won with the champion, not the decider. When the economic buyer asks a who question, answer with names and a plan on paper, not with plan tiers. If we don't have that plan as a standard asset, build it with your solutions engineer before the meeting rather than hoping the load test carries it. And read a one-word "good" from the decider as a warning, not a win.
